blocks.x: Bob Arburn, March 27th, 1957, Real 1. My name is Bob Arburn. Your name is Bob Campbell, right? Right. Bob Campbell. Hello, Bob. How are you? How are you? When were you born, Paul? Well, I tell you, I was born May the 5th. 1901.
Where? What part of this city?

I was born at New Orleans, Louisiana, at Barracks and St. Claude, right on the corner of Barracks and St. Claude. I did remember hearing Buddy Bowling because Buddy Bowling was playing a banquet at the place of Burns Hall. That's on Burrow between Annette and Seminole. And I was living on Equat in the back back back street from the Hall between Annette and Seminole. And Buddy was Buddy Bowling. The band was blowing. And the people was dancing, I imagine. And having a good time. My mom happened to call to say, that's Buddy Bowling blowing over there. That man sure can blow. That was about, let's see what year. I would say that was around 19... Six or seven. I was just a kid. I would say just about six or seven. I remember that. I can remember that.
That's a memory. Mm-hmm.

Anything else you remember around in there or later on? Later on? Yeah, they had a lot of things happen. Well, you see a millen boy. Gee, that was New Orleans. New Orleans was New Orleans at that time. You see, modern times, I mean, it changed everything. They had a lot of camps. Just like they have now in some parts of Littlewood. You know, out on the lake, the camp's out on the lake. Well, that's... It was flooded out there with camps. And people had picnics every day. Every day. And when they had a picnic, they had a band. And you'd hear a band. And this camp, and across the way, you hear another band. I mean, you'd look over there and see who was playing. Who was in that band? Well, some of the band was an organized band. And a lot of bands would just get-together bands. But it was good. You know, they knew what they was doing. You know, they knew the tunes. They had a beat. Did you go out there when you were young? Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. I went out there. I had a cousin that got killed by Smoke and Mirror. Smoke and Mirror was that old train used to run there. Run about five miles an hour. That was on Lidgetfield Street, which is Lidgetfield still there. And it was from Swampland in those days. And this boy was hopping on and hopping off. And he fell under the wheels and got killed. His name was Rogers. And when I was a young kid at that time, my grandmother used to give a lot of picnics at the lake. And they all used to have a good time. Everybody had a good time. All the time. They had so many camps. It was just New Orleans. New Orleans no more. I mean, it's a nice city. I mean, it's a beautiful city. But I'm speaking about the fun part of it. The fun part, everybody enjoyed themselves those days. I mean, many bands, they had all types of bands. They had colored bands, white bands. It was marvelous. All good bands. They had Christian's band. I think, I don't know if it was Emile Christian's brother or Emile himself had a band. Christian band. They played at the Lidgetfield and Dauphine a lot. They used to play on the gallery out there before they would go in. At that time, most of the band would play a couple of numbers on the gallery. You see, on the gallery before they would go inside, see, to let the people know that the band was there, you see. You mean out on the little porch around the gallery? Yeah, yeah. A little porch, yeah. A little porch, yeah. Well, it was a flight up. Always was a flight up, you know. Same as the dance halls, you know. They had you upstairs. They didn't have you down on the platform, down on the floor where you danced at. They had you up in the ceiling there. And it was really fun to sight. And they didn't use no piano in those days, you know. They used the band, the bass and the guitar, they used the banjo. But most of them used the guitars in those days. Because the first time I played with the piano in the band it felt funny to me. That's right, I was so used to playing with the bass and banjo, I couldn't get used to that. But you see in the red light district, well, they had pianos, you know what I mean. And just like Pete Lala, 101 Ranch, a few clothes, and so many other players. Ponce's plays, Henry Ponce's plays, Rice, over there in a lot of clubs. How did the bands sit in the old days? They were all in just a straight line.
The straight line on the bandstand, yeah. Well, you had the bass, then they had the guitar, the clarinet, the clarinet player, the trombone

and the drums. All in one line. Yeah, all in one line. The drums always on one end and the bass on the other. Yeah, man. Some bands, man. I wish I had a tape recorder, I'd be worth a billion dollars. Not a million, but I would be worth a billion dollars to catch those bands in those days. Must have been something to sit out there on a lake and hear them playing all over. Yeah, that's right. And you see like we sitting here right now, and we'd open this door and say you had a band at the Copper Raiders Hall right now, which is on a living between the St. Philp and the Maine, and the band would come out there and play about two or three tunes. Out in front of the hall? Yeah, in front of the hall. See, before they would go in, as I said before. Well, you could hear that band, you know, the wind would carry that band from there all the way here, I mean, which is about a mile and a half away I imagine. Isn't that right? It was about a mile and a half, you would say a mile and a half, I mean Copper Raiders Hall and that's something, you know what I mean. I was about 15, just about 15 years. That's a long time.
Did you play with any other kids before you had the drums? Well I used to be on the corners. Pick up group or anything?

No, I used to, I was the main attraction. I was always the main attraction. And the guys would have maybe a comb and they'd whistle. And I'd play the drums. At that time I got two sticks from the chairs, from the old chair, and I made the points on them, you know, playing out. What kind of whistle? Oh, just whistle, I mean it's like a whistle. Oh, you know, like a kid whistler. Yeah, just whistle, just whistle. Playing whistle without a whistle or a fife or anything like that. Where did you just play? Play up and down the street you mean? No, we'd go play on the corners, you know what I mean? The corners where we'd hang out at. We'd play on the corners where they'd hang out at. Cops would come and chase us away all the time. Make a lot of disturbing peace. Somebody would ring for the police and the cops would come on horseback and we'd see them. Ah, we'd be gone. We'd be gone. The horses didn't have no chance. Most of us would baffer anyway. They could run like rabbits. Did you know Dave DePas? Dave DePas? Yeah, he played with the Young Living Band later on in years, too. Which one?
The other one? Yeah, he played with the Young Living Band, buddy.
Yank Johnson. Oh, Yank Johnson. So, when did Chris Kelly die? That's one thing I remember. I can't recall what year that was. Was that before you went to Chicago, the first time?
No, I was in Chicago at the time, no. No, not the ... No, I was the second time.
I went to Chicago the second time. I would say in the 20s, you know.
He died in the 20s. Now what did Chris Kelly look like in the dress?
You know a guy that called Ike Play Trombone? He lives on Claymore Street. Don't you know a fellow called Ike?
Around Domain? That's right, yeah. I don't know. I heard about it.
He killed a fellow on the Fair Red Domain one time.
Big Ike.
Huh?
Is that the one?

Big Ike? Yeah, Big Ike, yeah. That's him? Yeah. Just like Chris Kelly. They said Chris Kelly had a lot of glow. All of his glow. All of his glow. Always smart. He's always smart. Did he wear expensive clothes? Well, he's a pretty neat guy. Don't make me terrible.
Old drummers, that is the first drummers that inspired you. People like Red Happy you were talking about.

Yeah, Red Happy. Just how they played? They had a lot of good drummers. Mike Murray was very sensational. Very good drummer. They had a tune that the band used to play. And they had a break. They used to make, you know, Mike Murray always carried a lot of contraptions with them, whistles and different kind of ratchets and all that for breaks, you know. And in this particular tune, he had a chain, you know, like they have on the wagons, a horse and wagon, a chain, a horse to the shaft. Well, they take this chain and lift it up and, and then in this rag that off of him, I can't recall what rag it was. They had a break. And he'd take and just drop that chain. Come out just perfect. He was a wonderful drummer. And anybody that's living today, which can recall, I'll tell you about, he was really a great drummer. Last time I heard him, he was playing on Rampart between Julia and the next street up at Howard, is it? Yeah, Howard. He's playing on the Rivertown side of the street upstairs. There's a face up there. He's playing with a four-piece band up there. Last time I heard Mike Murray, last time I can recall him.
How long ago was that?
Oh, man, I was, I was a kid, man. He's dead now.
He's been dead many years.
Oh, Mike Murray's been dead many years, yeah. Well, Mike Murray.
Baby Dodds used to talk about him too, that he inspired him. That was his favorite drummer. That's a good drummer.
Yeah, that's a good drummer.
Now, what kind of a drum set did he have? You say he used all things like chains and whistles and all.
Yeah, a lot of ratchets and things. Ratchets and all that. Yeah.
What kind of a snare drum did he have?

Well, he had, first time I seen him, he, and, well, last time I seen him too, he had the same drum. He had a, he had a, you know, a banjo, a banjo head, not a banjo head, just a banjo without the neck. And he had snares on that. Really?
Really?

That's what he had, that's right, real banjo, that's right. Really? That's what he had, that's right, real banjo, that's right. That's right, I'm not, I'm not, I'm telling you something I seen with these two.
I thought maybe they meant it was like a banjo. With the two eyes, huh? How's that? I thought they meant it was like a banjo, just a real thin snare gun, single head.

No, that's right, that's right, that's right. Well, how did he fit the snares on? I don't know, but. Was it the same side, he couldn't, he couldn't hit on top of the snares? Well, I don't know, I don't know how he had it, I don't know how he had it, but he had it. That's what he had it.
Yeah, that's what he had it. That's what he had it. It sounded, it tuned up pretty high then, or did you have it sort of loose?
Pretty high, no, it's pretty high, yeah, it's pretty high.
What kind of drum would he have, a bass drum?

Well, I don't remember the set, I mean, I couldn't recall, you know, what, what set it was, I mean. Well, most of the guys, that, that time, used, they had ropes on the bass drums, you know, you'd pull the ropes, you know, to tighten the drums, you know. Most of the guys had ropes on the bass drums, you know.
But would they have the same kind of foot pedal they got now?

No, no, no, no, no, no, they had, they had upright pedal, I mean, it come from the top, like on the ball and the ball and the ball and the ball and the ball. And the center, they had straps on them, see, and they had a spring down there. And which side? And the wooden, wooden, wooden pedal down there. How about that?
Which side of the bass drum would they hit on?
Well, on the same side of it, like you're playing now. Yeah. Yeah, I keep playing now.
They used tom-toms much in those days? Yeah, a little bit of tom-toms.
A little bit of tom-toms. A little bit of tom-toms.
A little bit of tom-toms. A little bit of Chinese.
Yeah, a little Chinese. Yeah, that's right, with all the nails of them, that's right.
How many cymbals? What cymbals?

Well, most of the guys used a little crash cymbals. Some guys had just a little cymbals, like you see when the guys beat, or playing the street parade, and I got on top of the drums. Yeah. Just a little bit of cymbals. A little chain, chain, chain. You know. A crash cymbals. No sounds, you know, nothing like that. Crash cymbals. Chinese? Yeah, yeah. Chinese crash was the main cymbal. How big was it? Well, some of them was 12 inches, I imagine. Well, they had them all sizes, I mean, in those days. Wood block? Wood block, yeah, and cob belts and them.
Who were the first people you saw play on the rim, or on the shell of the drum?
Oh, no. Who was the first one?
Or did they all do it, or I mean?
No, I think Baby Dots is about the one I can recall of me doing that. Baby Dots.
What about two beat and four beat and so on? Did they keep that bass drum boom, boom, boom going all the time?

No, you see, drummers like Mac Murray and Jean Vina, fellas, they never played no full beat. They played all those drummers played two beats. They never played no full beat. The first time I heard four beats played was King Oliver and O'Reilly was playing at the Columny Hall and Rain Happy was with the band. And they was playing the blues. And that's the first time I seen that full full beat. Full full. That's the first time I seen it playing the blues. And Happy was the first man that I see that used that. That's right.
And how did you happen to switch back to two beat? Who was that? Yourself. Myself?

Well I'll tell you why. She playing this kind of music, this Dixieland music. You see a lot of people are going to dance. If you start something, you say, you're going to dance. Okay, you're going out there to dance, the band playing. You see, well the people can't get no start. They couldn't get a start to dance. But if you, see they get the start, they're going there, you see what I mean? You see they get the beat. But if you start, people that are older poets wouldn't know where to start. You see but the people that, dance this kind of music, if you play two, I mean a start, two beat is a good beat. It's really a good beat that will move you. If you got a good bass man working with you that works, I mean you can play that two beat and really push a man. That's right.
What about Red Happy? When did he come up with? Who was that? Red Happy. I heard once he was like a kid with Louie and the Reform school. Well yeah. Louie's age or older?
Well I think Happy was older than Louie. Yeah, he's an older boy than Louie. What was his real name?
How was that?
What was his real name?
His name was Happy Bolton.

I mean Bolton was his last name. I don't know. Let's see if I can call his name. I didn't know it. Happy Bolton. I don't know his name was Bolton Bure or whatever you want. Lee Collins told me he used to do a lot of scat singing. He was a rock band. Yeah, he did a lot of scat singing. Yeah, he was a sensational drummer. He was a sensational drummer. He was uncool though. He'd come and pick up your stick. Give me a stick. You don't know what you're doing. You might play something. Just like that. You know, just take your stick out there. That's right.
You know, just take your stick out there. That's right. You know, just take your stick out there. That's right. You know, I didn't know it.

I didn't know it. I didn't know it. I have a Bolton. I know his name was Bolton Bure or whatever you want. He was a tough boy, man. He kept getting a belly. Yeah, he was a tough boy, man. He kept getting a belly. Yeah. He was a professional drummer. He was a professional drummer. He was uncool though. He was uncool though. He'd come and pick up your stick. Give me a stick. You didn't know what you were doing. You might play something. Just like that. You know, just take your stick out there. That's a bully. You know. I used to feel sorry the way you do Mac. Pull on Mac Lacey. You borrow Mac Lacey's drum and a cymbal or anything. Never give it back to him, man. Dan would say anything. He was tough, man. He didn't give, man. He didn't give it back to him. He was tough, man. He didn't give it back to him. He didn't give it back to him. He didn't fool with Benny. No, he didn't fool with Benny. No, Benny. Benny was another character, man. See, Benny would be playing the parade and somebody would do something that he knew. He'd forget all about the parade. Start a big fight, man. Put the bass drum down and start the fighting. The character, man. He hit you at that mallet. If you got too close to the bass drumming, like the people doing that getting close to enjoying the music and all between, he'd take that mallet and hit you in the head with
it. Get out of the way. He didn't hear. I guess that stopped the parade, wouldn't it? Yeah.

They tell me a lot of times that in BG when they go ask the warden, don't let him come out and play the parade, man. Come out and play the parade and go back in. He was well liked in the prison. Well, that's all he did. He was mischief.
He was like to never miss a beat and hit somebody on the head. I imagine so.

He didn't kill. Then he had to go and get killed after he turned out to be a nice quiet guy. He was quiet. What happened to him? Well, some girl killed him up on the ground. Franklin, grabbing Franklin. Kill him on the corner.
Now, who did Bolton play with? Did he say he played even with Oliver and then? Yeah, he played with Oren and Oliver. Thank you.
Yeah, he played with Oren and Oliver.
I'll take seven up a drink. Unless somebody else wants to. Is that your favorite drink, Paul? The water. Oh, no. How much you want to miss it?
You drink water?
No, I'll get to the drink right now.
Little Russ channel. Thanks, Raymond.
What did you say about Happy?

Oh, different ones he played with or anything else about his style of playing? Because that fellow never recorded and nobody knows anything about him much either. Like Lacey, I wondered what style they played. Did you tell anything more about the type of drums and all they played?

Well, I would say my kid brother plays something on her Lacey. He plays smooth, you know what I mean? He's not rough at all. Lacey was a much better drummer than my brother. I admire him. I admire him. All the old timers and all the drummers are. Still to say I'll take Mac Lacey.
Which nobody knew.
The thing I probably don't know about is mentioned. Maybe David Osweiler might mention.
Yeah, I think Roy Palmer talked about him once. Nice, nice day. He couldn't remember his last name. Said his name was Mac.
Yeah, he tried a lot with Mac and Mac.
Yeah.

Yeah, I remember. He was on the show together. Did you call him Little Mac? Yeah, Mac Lacey. Yeah, Little Mac, yeah. Little Mac, I heard him. Little Mac, yeah. Little Mac, yeah. I never knew his last name. Yeah, a few people talked about him. I'm in trouble, man. I wish he would have been calling him. I mean, I wish he'd heard him, man.
What about that old man, Cottrell?

Oh, he was one of the best street drummers, you know. No one liked him. What did he play in the street? He played a snare drum. He heard that snare drum, you heard a snare drum, my boy. Like them guys today, man. He heard them drums. Oh man, he played like them fellas played up there, man. There's nothing, nothing happened with them fellas, man. I'm the only guy, you know what I mean, trying to imitate him. That's right. I mean, a lot of people hear the drums, man. Play a whisper, keep a secret. No secret on the street, no. No secret, man. No secret drum, man. The fellas had no license with them drums, man.
Well, how did he work with a bass drummer, man? How did the bass drum and the snails work in the street? Would he work steady with one guy, would they work up things or not together?

No, well, look, Cottrell, he played with the Excelsior band all the time, you know. And the Jaws was the bass drum player. I didn't like the way Jaws played. He was playing good marches and things. Marches played a band, terrific playing the marches. I hate to say that, but I didn't like the way he played bass drum. He didn't play the police beat, because he didn't play the jazz beats. He didn't play the strings. You know, he played the strings, you know, boom, boom, jump, jump, jump, like that. And the mother felt, boom, boom, you know, feel it, you know. Everybody screaming in the streets, you know. People want your arm, man. They don't want your arm. Who were the best bass drummers that you think? Well, who was the best bass drum player? I wouldn't say Black Benny, man, because Black Benny is overrated. No, I wouldn't say that, man. He was all right. I mean, as far as that, Ray Allen played as much bass drum, I think, as Black Benny played, you know, around the same time when Benny was living. Who was it?
Ray Allen. Which one? You mean the young one? Yeah, Ray Allen. Sonny Allen.

Sonny Allen. Sonny Allen played as much bass drum as Black Benny. I mean, the guy just, I mean, Black Benny just was a guy that, well, I would say that was knowing and thinking that between these fighting and hitting somebody in the mouth or something like that, and he got a reputation, everybody said, Black Benny, Black Benny, but I could never see where Black Benny was greater than Jean Vigne. And Jean Vigne was a wonderful bass drum player. And Brian Strapania, I mean, bass drum players, I mean, there was no comparison. I mean, with those two guys, I mean, he was good. All right. Black Benny got a reputation. I go, he got that reputation. I go, he got that reputation. What? Because I watched him. And at the time I was playing him, you know, so I was working at Tom Madison at the time.
Well, what about Nenya, or someone like that? Well, Mr. Pandon. Mr. Pandon was wonderful.
That's the bass drum player.
Would he play a straight four beat in the street, or would he play a two beat?
No, he played a four beat in the street like they do in the day of me. And he put in a lot of accents. Yeah, it looks like a beat, yeah. Well, he put in all that double rap.
Yeah, yeah, he played with all the double rap.
That's right. Could you give me a sample on your leg?
Huh? Can you give me a sample on your leg like that or something? What? Light sounding? You need a bass drum. Could you give me a beat? Well, a hard sound, yeah. Mm-hmm.
That, that, which one I played?
Just give me the bass drum.

That, that, that, that, that, that, that, that, that, that, that, that, that, that, that, that, that, that, that, that, that, that, that, that, that, that, that, that, that, that, that, that. That way he played? Yeah, I got that idea. That's the way he played. Oh, boom, boom, boom, boom. Oh, boy. Good job, man. What's up, Bill? I gotta run along. I gotta get out of the school in 15 minutes. Oh, boy.

Thought you were gonna talk some with you guys. Can I ask all the questions? No, they didn't all ask you, and Bob, they'll think plenty of things. They wanted to hear you talk a lot about parades and funerals and things, anything like that. And then your days when you went to Chicago. They're not gonna work you to death, but I mean, you can tell a little bit about when you went to Chicago and played with Oliver and Louie and all that stuff, too.
Well, it was wonderful, wonderful days, I mean. Yeah. It was wonderful days. Chicago, Chicago.

Which I'm just saying here, I'll listen to the tape later and get all this. Yeah, Chicago, Chicago, there are days, I mean. So, I think I better run along now. Bob, why don't you move over there and watch that? Yeah, I'll watch it. If you can reach down there and watch the level sometimes, it's working pretty good.
How far you gotta go? You gotta go in good ways, you want me to take it?

No, no, it's not far, up in Gentelling Hill. I can be there in 15 minutes. I can take it, no. Oh, no, no, thanks. Be back in the Jifford. No, I can get the bus right there and be there in five minutes. See, the band don't want me to take it. I can take it, man. There's some more tape in the box, you know, there's a couple of things. Okay.
Well, in this front line, I thought...
Oh, see, I meant something tonight.
You're still at the dream room tonight, huh? You don't have to force yourself to come there. Just take your rest. Because you need some rest. You know how to come there. I'll see you today.
I'll tell the boy I'm not seeing you. I'll tell you all right. All right, Bill, glad seeing you.
Bill, he's a nice guy. Marvelous. One of the finest guys, boy, in existence. That's right, boy. He sure is. He's a fine man, boy. You said Bill got a girlfriend, you think? Brossel?
Yeah.
And he got a girlfriend? Is Bill going to get married, you think? No. You don't think Bill's going to get married? Not for a while.
Huh? Not for a while. He might be cool and secret, you can't tell. He got two birds.
He got two boy heads. They keep me busy enough pecking at you. Yeah, yeah, yeah.

You guys have a friend that come, you might understand, but I don't think she's too serious about a mental thing. I don't know. But anyway, back to what we were talking about. I was wondering how people dressed for funerals and parades.

Oh, in those days, well, they had uniforms. All the bands had uniforms. They had blue uniforms. One band I seen had, you know, no, I wouldn't say one band, no. Because the Eagle Band, I mean, I mean the band, not the brass band, the Eagle Band. The orchestra. The orchestra. They had a green outfit with black, I call them, black design.
Green coats, green trots with black design. Like those frogs on the ground? Yeah, yeah, that's right.
All the bands had that, see. All the bands. When you get it.
Was this just a green suit, or was it more like a tuxedo or something? No, no, just straight, you know. All the bands.

Yeah, like a band uniform. All the bands wore it. What kind of cloth? Just regular. Oh, well, it was good material. Very good material, yeah. It wasn't all on. It wasn't velvet or anything like that. No, no, it wasn't velvet, no. It didn't have no velvet, no lapels or anything like that. It just was some kind of a braid, I mean, I recall. You know how they do, I mean. That was beautiful, I mean, because all the bands, you know. I remember the band had the same thing, you know, uniform. They bought uniform, you know, it was organized brass bands. Like the OBBs, the OBB and Excelsior. Well, that was two main bands they had, you know.
OBB is on one? On one brass bands.
Did those collars come up tight?
Did they wear ties or did the coat button up all the way to the back? The coat button all the way, that's right. Coat button all the way.
Well, did they wear a band?

They had a tie, you know, a dog tie against the street tie, yeah. But the first time you couldn't see the tie because of all the other clothes. It was wonderful, huh? Did they wear a band? I have a picture. Oh, you've seen the… You mean I tell about you, you've seen a brass band with those hunter collars? Coats and pictures?
Yeah, I've seen it, but I want you to tell me about it. I don't know if the picture's right. It might be just one picture and they might have had another band dressed entirely different, you know.
Were the coats very long or were they just sort of ordinary like?
No, they're so ordinary coats like, like you have the what size of the wrench you have. I mean, yeah. Coat that would look, you know, look presentable.
Would they wear the same cap for parade or they'd wear for a funeral, for example? Yeah, they did.

I mean, they didn't like today, I mean, you see. They'd wear the dog caps, you see me. Same uniform. But today, you see, they wear a white cap for parade and for a funeral, they wear a dog cap today, you see me. But the guys haven't got no uniform. I haven't got guys come up with blue pants or something. Anyway, if they had a black pants and a white shirt or even a blue shirt, and all I should say a blue shirt for parade, and a white top or a cap and a black pants and black shoes. The guys come out with tans, shoes, and they come with a gray pants, they don't look nice, you know what I mean? They don't, it looks raggedy, you know, like, but if all the guys had, that's what I'm trying to tell John Cashman, why don't you know, you tell all the fellas by a pair of black, a good pair of black trousers, a couple of pair of black trousers. When you come out, you know everybody looks, looks like in dark black shoes, you know, white cap, I mean, and then it looks like a man going up the street, you know, coming, coming, or going.

Paul Barberin, March 27, 1957, reel 2. Was there any braid on the trousers or was it just on the colors? No, it was on the side. On the side, like a tuxedo. Yeah, I like a tuxedo, that's right. It was really nice.
Did the band ever wear aprons like the mumboe did?
No, no. No, I've never wore that, no. I don't know, like the Masonics and anything? No, no, no. In the old days who wore aprons?
What kind of aprons did they have? Did the Masonics or the others? The Masonic and our art fellas and Michael O'Groen Schumer and those people like that. What dance?

Oh no, on Labor Day, Labor Day Parade. Labor Day Parade was a parade. That was another nice parade. They'd have all the bands out. All the bands. They were bands they could get. They could see a parade. And those things were never coming back no more. Where would the parade start and end up? Or like the Labor Day Parade? Well, Labor Day Parade, well, I'll tell you as far as I know about it, Labor Day Parade would start at the River Canal, right on that part. And they'd come down, come around Cloud Street. I mean, down in Ramport to Espinade. segments.title: Birth in 1901 and hearing Buddy Bolden at age six or seven
segments.summary: Barbarin gives his birth date and place and recalls hearing Buddy Bolden's band across from his home as a small child.

segments.title: Lake camps, picnic bands and bands playing on the gallery
segments.summary: He remembers lakefront camps with bands every day, his cousin killed by the lake train, bands playing on the gallery before dances, and pianos only in the red-light district.

segments.title: How old-time bands sat in a straight line
segments.summary: The interviewer and Barbarin describe the seating order of early bands, and how a band's tunes carried a mile and a half in the wind.

segments.title: Banging on chairs as a kid and street-corner groups
segments.summary: As a boy he drummed with chair sticks while friends whistled on street corners, chased off by mounted police; Dave DePas and Yank Johnson come up.

segments.title: Chris Kelly's death and Big Ike
segments.summary: Talk about when Chris Kelly died, his sharp dress, and a trombonist called Big Ike who killed a man.

segments.title: Mike Murray, the sensational early drummer
segments.summary: Barbarin describes Mike Murray's novelty breaks with chains and ratchets and the last time he heard him.

segments.title: Early drum sets: banjo-shell snare, rope bass drums, pedals and cymbals
segments.summary: Details of the snare, bass drum ropes and pedals, tom-toms, Chinese cymbals and wood blocks used by early New Orleans drummers.

segments.title: Two-beat versus four-beat bass drum playing
segments.summary: Who first played rim shots and a full four beat (Red Happy with Oliver), and why Barbarin returned to a two-beat for dancers.

segments.title: Red Happy Bolton and Black Benny as drummers
segments.summary: Barbarin recalls Happy Bolton's scat singing and bullying, and the fighting bass drummer Black Benny and his death.

segments.title: Mac Lacey, the little drummer nobody can place
segments.summary: After a break for drinks, they discuss Mac Lacey's smooth style compared with his brother and who else remembers him.

segments.title: Old Cottrell and Jaws in the Excelsior band
segments.summary: Cottrell as the great street snare drummer, and Barbarin's dislike of Jaws's bass drumming.

segments.title: Black Benny overrated; other bass drummers and a demonstration
segments.summary: He ranks bass drummers: Sonny Allen, Jean Vigne and others against Black Benny, and taps out a street bass drum beat.

segments.title: Russell leaves; talk of Chicago and social chatter
segments.summary: The interviewers say what they want covered, one leaves, and there is small talk before the questions resume.

segments.title: Brass band and Eagle Band uniforms, caps and trousers
segments.summary: Description of band uniforms in the old days, the Eagle Band's green outfits, and complaints about mismatched uniforms today.

segments.title: Braid on trousers, aprons and the Labor Day Parade route
segments.summary: Reel 2 begins with uniform braid, then Barbarin describes the Labor Day Parade and its route.

segments.title: How pleasure club members dressed for parades
segments.summary: Pleasure clubs bought new outfits each year: striped silk shirts, soft white hats and badges.

segments.title: Umbrellas, baskets and the Grand Marshal's streamer
segments.summary: Paper umbrellas with streamers, baskets of flowers and cigars, and how the Grand Marshal dressed differently.

segments.title: Garvey-style hats and his uncle's plumed brass band hats
segments.summary: Comparison to Marcus Garvey's uniform, plumed hats worn by his uncle's band before his time, and unrecalled basket decorations.

segments.title: Funeral hearse, black horses and horse shrouds
segments.summary: The old horse-drawn hearse, its decorations, the black shrouds on the horses and what they cost.

segments.title: Order of the funeral procession
segments.summary: Who walked and who rode in carriages, and where the band, members, priest and hearse fit in the funeral line.

segments.title: Societies hiring bands, second liners and sticks
segments.summary: Every society had music; second liners, their sticks, and swords and fights between wards.

segments.title: Funeral tunes: Didn't He Ramble, hymns and Bourbon Street Parade
segments.summary: Which pieces were appropriate on the way to and from the cemetery, and the idea of recording a real brass band.

segments.title: Assembling a recording brass band and saxes in brass bands
segments.summary: Possible personnel for a recording brass band, and why saxophones are used in bands now.

segments.title: Relief drumming in the district and Blue Monday at the 25
segments.summary: He relieved Cottrell at Rice, Zeno at Pete Lala's and others, and recalls the ham-kicking contest at the 25.

segments.title: Monday society banquets and dances
segments.summary: Societies gave Monday afternoon banquets at halls, each with a band.

segments.title: His uncle Louis Arthidore and his father in the Onward Brass Band
segments.summary: His uncle was a fine clarinetist; his father played cornet then alto in the same brass band.

segments.title: Barbarin brothers, nephew Danny Barker and the family of musicians
segments.summary: He lists his brothers, sister Rose's son Danny Barker, and nephews who play trumpet and trombone.

segments.title: Quiet old New Orleans, its bands and the 'Kid' nicknames
